records.name: Niue
records.current_summary:
One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of New Zealand; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust history of criminalisation, Niue section: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May (in force June), removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' — offences under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code carrying up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand via 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation (which changed NZ law only). For this record: documented legal decriminalisation and its colonial-law chain.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

GayLawNet Niue laws page: age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors); the age of consent was reportedly equalised in May 2011 (per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia, May 2011); the page flags limited information available on Niue topics. For this record: dated consent-equality and the sex-asymmetric age of majority still on the books.

records.name: Hong Kong
records.current_summary:
A special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement: trans claims here have been fought in court more than legislated. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the apex court in 2023 ruled full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a precondition for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card — reversing a 2019 high-court loss in the same litigation. Beyond the card, however, recognition still runs on surgery; and where the executive has chosen, it has chosen against: in September 2025 the legislature voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, so relationship recognition and any SOGI equality ordinance remain absent.

Corporate visibility invites backlash (a bank's rainbow installations drew a homophobic campaign in 2016), and open activism operates in a space tightened since the 2020 security law. Visitor arithmetic: no criminal law, dense urban anonymity, a functioning marker-change route on cards — inside a system that still demands surgery for most recognition and whose politicians recently voted inclusion down.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of China; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: AP (Feb 2023): 'Hong Kong transgender men win appeal over status change' — the Court of Final Appeal rules full sex-reassignment surgery should not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on official identity cards, a far-reaching win in the Henry Tse case.

PinkNews (1 Feb 2019): HK High Court ruled against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R — Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion', rejecting self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain; counsel called the requirement 'out of proportion'. Current status per freshness: legal gender recognition still requires full sex-reassignment surgery; Sept 2025 LegCo voted the government's registered-partnerships bill down 71-14.

HKFP opinion by Nury Vittachi (7 Dec 2016), 'HSBC's rainbow lions: Can we have our homophobia back please?': documents the 2016 backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations — a viral local campaign insisting homophobia is homegrown or foreign-imported, framed satirically. Useful as climate evidence: corporate LGBT visibility provokes organised pushback in Hong Kong.

HK Court of Appeal, Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions setting the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 vs 16 for heterosexual acts — the applicant (21, in same-sex relationships since 16) argued the disparity unjustifiably discriminated; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality. Landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

freshness_all.fact: LegCo VETOED the government's registered-partnerships bill 71–14 (Sept 2025) after the Sep-2025 court deadline; legal gender recognition still requires full sex reassignment surgery

records.name: Macau
records.current_summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.
records.current_outOfScope: Territory of China; local deviations noted in summary.

sources.claim: Macau Daily Times (Feb 2015): Rainbow of Macau met Identification Bureau officials to discuss changing gender on Macau ID documents - one individual ('Avery', speaking behind a screen) sought the change; the first organised push for gender recognition in Macau.

Macau Daily Times (May 2016): Rainbow of Macau criticised the government for excluding same-sex relationships from domestic-violence legislation because same-sex partners were not considered 'family members'.

Jason Chao / Rainbow of Macau statement (May 2016): the government knowingly enacted a discriminatory domestic-violence law despite the UN Committee against Torture's 2015 concluding observations requiring protection without discrimination; warns the law signals that sexual-orientation discrimination is justifiable.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Macau
sources.claim: Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Macau': same-sex activity decriminalised 1996; no recognition of same-sex unions; Basic Law Art. 25 discrimination list omits sexual orientation — SOGI protection only in employment (Law 7/2008 Art. 6/2); the 2012 domestic-violence draft dropped same-sex cohabitants for 'lack of social consensus'; the 2015 gender-marker-change study never produced a law.

sources.title: Transgenders don't exist in the eyes of the law
sources.claim: Plataforma Media (8 Sep 2023): transgender residents cannot change sex on Macau ID cards — no data-change policy exists — causing border-crossing confusion (a trans man holding a Hong Kong card marked male is still registered female in Macau); activists press the long-promised legislative reform.

sources.title: Macau: legal recognition of gender identity requires 'prudent study'
sources.claim: Plataforma Media (7 Apr 2026): the Justice Services Direction (DSAJ) says gender-identity legal recognition still needs 'prudent study' of core societal values, civil and family law, and states there are 'no plans to revise the framework' — Macau remains the only area in China without ID gender-marker change or sex-reassignment provisions (both possible in mainland China and Hong Kong), despite a 31 March 2026 appeal by four trans residents.

records.name: Western Sahara
records.current_summary:
A disputed North African territory under military administration by a neighbouring state, whose penal code governs any visitor: same-sex intimacy is criminalised (six months to three years) with wide police discretion, and morality articles are the tool turned on visibly trans people — rights reviews document involuntary outing, expression discrepancies at checkpoints and registries, no gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition (a 2021 path covers intersex people only); the administering state's religious establishment has condemned transition.

Occupation stacks the risk: 170 charged in the administering state in one year, a 2020 organised outing campaign, rights defenders tried at the territory's own court (a 2005 case of eight Sahrawis remains a landmark), and a 2018 legal study recording LGBTI Sahrawis exposed to violations by state and non-state actors alike. For an outed visitor: criminalisation, morality enforcement and occupation policing, with no civil space and negligible accountability.
records.current_outOfScope: Disputed territory; see Morocco entry for the underlying legal analysis.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch dispatch (9 Dec 2005): trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests; HRW called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. Documents Moroccan state authority exercised over the territory (security services, courts) and detention of Sahrawi activists - the legal framework a visitor to the territory stands under.

PinkNews global legality roundup (Jul 2017): lists the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic as a jurisdiction where homosexuality is illegal for men and women, noting it has been illegal for decades and that the partially-recognised state (AU member since 2016) governs the territory claim. Date-stamps the 2017 status as criminalised.
